div.head: V Atr 28
div.ab: ⁊ gyf hwa butan leafe of fyrde gewende, þe se cyning sylf on sy, plihte him sylfum ⁊ ealre his are.
⁊ gif hwa butan leafe of fyrde gewende, þe se cyning sylf on sy, plihte him sylfum oððe wergylde.
And gif hwa buton leafe of firde gewænde þe se cyningc silf on sy, plihte him silfum oððe wergilde.
And gyf hwa butan leafe of fyrde gewende þe se cyning sylf on sy, plihte him sylfum and ealre his are.
And if anyone deserts an army which is under the personal command of the king, it shall be at the risk of [losing] his life or his wergeld.
And if anyone deserts an army led by the king himself, he shall risk forfeiture of his life and all his property.
And if anyone deserts without leave from an army which the king himself is with, it is to be at the peril of his life and all his property.
Und wenn jemand ohne Erlaubniss von der Landwehr, bei der der König selbst ist, fortgeht, bringe er seinem Leben und seiner Besitzstellung (oder seinem Wergeld G2 D) Verwirkungsgefahr.
And if anyone leaves the army without permission when the king himself is with it, let him put at risk his life and his whole property (or his wergild, G2 D).
div.note: In VI Atr 35, ‘his are’ without danger to life; II Cn 77 threatens property and life. Perhaps ‘oððe wergilde’ stood in the margin of the archetype (Liebermann).
The other MSS allow wergild instead of this heavy penalty; VI Ethelred 35 drops the death penalty.
and ealre his are: oððe wergylde G2D
all his property: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 replaces this phrase with “or his wergild.”
